overview:
Hungary is a landlocked country in Central Europe, about the size of Indiana, spread across a wide, flat basin ringed by the Carpathian Mountains of its neighbors. The Danube River flows through the middle and splits the capital, Budapest, into hilly Buda on the west bank and flat, busy Pest on the east, joined by graceful bridges and watched over by a huge parliament building on the river. Budapest is famous for grand cafés, a century-old subway, and steaming thermal baths fed by more than a hundred hot springs.

About 9.6 million people live in Hungary. Their language, Hungarian, or Magyar, is unlike any of its neighbors' tongues; its closest relatives are Finnish and Estonian, and its ancestors came from the Ural Mountains more than a thousand years ago. Hungary is a parliamentary republic and has been a member of the European Union since 2004. Farms on the plains grow wheat, corn, sunflowers, and the paprika peppers that color Hungarian cooking, and factories build cars and electronics. Hungarians are proud inventors, from the ballpoint pen to the Rubik's Cube.
landAndNature: Most of Hungary is the Great Hungarian Plain, or Alföld, a flat expanse of farmland and grassland stretching east of the Danube; the Hortobágy, a vast steppe, is grazed by gray longhorn cattle and shaggy racka sheep with spiral horns, and herders there still ride horses in traditional style. The Danube and the Tisza are the great rivers. Low mountains rise in the north, with Kékes at 1,014 meters the highest point. Lake Balaton in the west is the largest lake in Central Europe, a shallow, warm summer playground for swimmers and sailors, and Lake Hévíz nearby is one of the world's largest natural thermal lakes. Caves honeycomb the Aggtelek karst. Great bustards, among the heaviest flying birds, stride across the plains, and storks nest on village poles.
peopleAndCulture: Hungarian food is hearty and red with paprika: goulash, a beef and vegetable soup, chicken paprikash with dumplings, stuffed cabbage, and lángos, fried dough topped with sour cream and cheese. Sweets include Dobos torte and chimney cakes roasted over coals. Most Hungarians are Christian, mainly Catholic or Reformed. Folk dance and the fiery music of Gypsy violin bands are national treasures, and composers Franz Liszt, Béla Bartók, and Zoltán Kodály drew on folk melodies. Soaking in thermal baths, some in ornate art nouveau buildings, is a weekly ritual, and chess games are played in the pools. Hungary has won more Olympic medals per person than almost any nation, especially in water polo, fencing, swimming, and canoeing.
history: Around 895 the Magyars, horse-riding warriors from the east, swept into the Carpathian Basin under their leader Árpád. King Stephen I made Hungary a Christian kingdom in the year 1000. The medieval kingdom was powerful until the Ottoman Turks won the Battle of Mohács in 1526 and occupied central Hungary for 150 years. The Habsburgs of Austria then ruled, and after a failed revolution in 1848 Hungary became an equal partner in Austria-Hungary in 1867. Defeat in World War I cost Hungary two-thirds of its territory. Hungary was allied with Nazi Germany in World War II, and about half a million Hungarian Jews were murdered in the Holocaust. Soviet forces installed a communist government, and an uprising in 1956 was crushed by Soviet tanks. Communism ended in 1989, and Hungary joined NATO in 1999 and the EU in 2004.
funFacts: The Rubik's Cube was invented in 1974 by Hungarian architecture professor Ernő Rubik, who took a month to solve it himself.
Budapest has more thermal springs than any other capital city, with about 120 feeding its famous baths.
The ballpoint pen was patented by Hungarian journalist László Bíró in 1938, and pens are still called biros in many countries.
Hungarian has 14 vowels and words like megszentségteleníthetetlenségeskedéseitekért, 44 letters long.
Budapest's underground railway, opened in 1896, was the first electric subway on the European mainland.
